analysis.one_liner: Lets wealthy families pay a 1% annual income surcharge for seven years instead of the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors, was never considered by the Ways and Means Committee, and died when the 113th Congress ended without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let any taxpayer choose, permanently and irrevocably, to stop paying the federal estate tax and generation-skipping transfer tax. In their place, they would pay an extra 1% of their yearly income for at least seven years. When someone who made the election dies, their heirs would inherit assets with the deceased's original cost basis (the lower of what they paid or what it was worth at death), so the family would owe capital gains tax later when they sell — but no estate tax up front. It was introduced in the final weeks of a two-year Congress and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of very large estates. Someone with a large estate but a comparatively modest annual income could replace a tax charged against their whole estate at death with a small annual levy of 1% of income for seven years — potentially paying a small fraction of what the estate tax would cost. The bill's own findings point to estates above the roughly $5 million exemption level as the ones affected [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Electing taxpayers stop paying both the estate tax and the generation-skipping transfer tax, and instead pay an additional 1% of adjusted gross income each year, with a minimum seven-year commitment [S2][S3].

Heirs of electing decedents get carry-over basis — the lesser of the deceased's original cost or the value at death — so untaxed appreciation is taxed later as capital gains rather than being hit with an estate tax at death [S3].

The bill's findings argue the estate tax forces family businesses, farms, and ranches to be sold to pay the tax, and notes the tax raised about $14 billion in fiscal 2013, under half a percent of IRS collections [S3].
The bill offers a transition deal for 2015–2016 elections: a decedent who dies before completing seven years can settle up with a make-up payment instead of losing the election entirely [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury, and ultimately other taxpayers, if elected estates pay far less than the estate tax would have collected on them. Ordinary families without large estates gain nothing, since their estates are already below the exemption and electing would simply add seven years of extra tax for them.

drawbacks.text: The math favors only the very wealthy: the estate tax is charged against the entire estate above the exemption, while the substitute is 1% of yearly income for seven years, so a family whose wealth vastly exceeds its income could pay a small fraction of the tax it owed before. The bill asserts the swap would be revenue-neutral but the text contains no mechanism guaranteeing that [S3].

The election is irrevocable and requires at least seven years of payments; someone who dies sooner must pay a make-up tax, and married couples must file jointly under the regime, adding risk and complexity for electors [S3].

The bill replaces one set of rules with another: it creates new executor information returns, annual beneficiary asset returns, and penalties of up to $10,000 per failure (5% of property value for intentional disregard), so the promised simplification comes with its own compliance burden [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a small group of very wealthy families, the math is highly favorable: a levy capped at 1% of annual income for seven years is far smaller than a tax on the entire estate at death. For everyone else the trade is bad — the promised revenue neutrality is asserted in the bill's findings but not built into the design, so the general taxpayer would bear the shortfall. The bill was also introduced with no cosponsors in the closing days of a Congress, which is a poor way to advance a major restructuring of the tax code.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended three weeks later.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Harris introduced the bill on December 11, 2014, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S1][S5].

The only further action was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on December 12, 2014; the committee never acted, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, killing the bill [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Treasury and ordinary taxpayers are better off, because the estate tax remained in place rather than being replaced by an elective levy that large estates could pay at a steep discount. Wealthy families who might have elected the cheaper regime gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Andy Harris
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor record

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Dave Camp (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan split ever took shape; the bill died quietly in committee with a Republican sponsor and a Republican-run committee.

industries.note: An electing family could replace a tax charged against its entire estate above the exemption with 1% of annual income for seven years — a steep discount for households whose wealth dwarfs their income. Their gain would be the Treasury's loss.

The bill's findings say the estate tax forces sales of family businesses and farms to pay the tax [S3]. In practice the estate tax already exempts estates up to roughly $5 million, so the overwhelming majority of these businesses never owed it in the first place; the main beneficiaries would be the largest ones.

A simplified elective regime would reduce some estate-planning and valuation work, but the bill creates new executor information returns, annual beneficiary returns, and penalties up to $10,000 per failure, generating a new compliance workload.
